name: Tommy Tuberville
summary: The incumbent U.S. senator supports data center development in communities that want it and opposes tax breaks. He sponsored federal legislation encouraging consumer protections and requiring large energy users to cover their energy costs; the bill failed in the Senate.

name: Doug Jones
summary: The former U.S. senator has proposed a one-year pause on new data center projects to establish safeguards. He opposes tax breaks for the facilities. His stance on qater-use reporting, power regulations and noise assessments remain unclear.

name: Bernadette Wilson
summary: The entrepreneur has said she would not allow hyperscale data centers that consume Alaska’s resources and damage its land, according to reporting from the Alaska Beacon. Her position on a moratorium remains unclear. Her campaign website does not provide a detailed data center policy, and she has had limited public comment on the issue.

name: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins
summary: The former state legislator and science-and-technology adviser supports local approval and requiring AI companies to cover their electricity costs. He proposes a statewide moratorium until lawmakers establish a regulatory framework. He has acknowledged noise concerns should be addressed but not disclosed how he would address them. His position on tax incentives remains unclear.

name: Andy Biggs
summary: The U.S. representative opposes tax incentives and says data centers should produce their own energy. He has called for accurate measurement and reporting of groundwater levels, but has not specified his stance on public water-use reporting. He opposes a statewide moratorium on data center projects.

name: Katie Hobbs
summary: The incumbent supports requiring data centers to pay their share of utility costs and ending tax incentives. She is concerned about neighborhood impacts but does not support a statewide moratorium. Her position remains unclear on noise assessment requirements public reporting of water use.

name: Sarah Huckabee Sanders
summary: The incumbent has welcomed data center development and legislation creating and expanding tax incentives, but her position on issuing a moratorium remains unclear. A spokesperson said she helped oppose efforts to prevent states from regulating AI or data centers, but the campaign did not directly answer the project’s questions.

name: Frederick Love
summary: The term-limited state senator supports a moratorium to establish standards and says the state should not actively invest to attract data centers. He voted for legislation expanding data center tax incentives, indicating support for those breaks.

name: Steve Hilton
summary: The former political adviser supports growing California’s AI industry and opposes a statewide moratorium. He says data centers should contribute to local communities and has criticized excessive noise, but has not outlined specific noise rules. His broader data center policy remains limited.

name: Xavier Becerra
summary: The former U.S. health and human services secretary says data centers should cover their energy costs and support local infrastructure and economies. He wants the industry to grow under environmental performance disclosure standards, though he has not specified those requirements. He also supports a more predictable permitting process.

name: Victor Marx
summary: At an Oct. 8 debate, the candidate said decisions about data centers should be left to local communities and described them as an economic boost. The campaign did not respond to requests for comment.

name: Phil Weiser
summary: The state attorney general has tied data center policy to climate goals and supports public reporting of water use. He opposes a statewide moratorium and has indicated support for tax incentives in some circumstances.

name: Ryan Fazio
summary: The state senator opposes data center tax incentives and has proposed repealing them. He supports requiring facilities to provide and pay for their own electricity and favors local control over siting. He has said he is not calling for a moratorium or ban on data centers. Clear positions on public water-use reporting and noise assessments were not identified.

name: Ned Lamont
summary: The incumbent signed off on tax incentives in the past but has openly opposed hyperscale AI data centers and criticized the electricity and water demands of large facilities. He has called for slowing new development unless projects add power generation, but not for an outright moratorium. Clear positions on a statewide moratorium, public water-use reporting and noise assessments were not identified.

name: Byron Donalds
summary: The U.S. representative supports requiring data centers to cover their utility costs and comply with water-use requirements. In July, he introduced House Bill 9777, the "Protecting Ratepayers Act," which mandated data centers use off-grid power generation and non-public water supply. He opposes a statewide moratorium and favors local control over siting. Positions on public water-use reporting, tax incentives and noise assessments are unclear.

name: David Jolly
summary: The former U.S. representative supports a one-year statewide moratorium to study environmental and community impacts. He has raised concerns about water and electricity use and criticized existing tax breaks. He views requiring facilities to cover utility costs as a first step but says more protections are needed. Specific positions on water reporting and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Rick Jackson
summary: The business executive opposes a statewide moratorium and favors local decision-making. He has proposed a three-part test focused on community support, environmental standards and relief from local costs. The campaign did not respond to questions.

name: Keisha Lance Bottoms
summary: The former Atlanta mayor has proposed a moratorium on new data centers to assess their costs and environmental impacts. Public positions on water reporting, utility requirements, tax incentives and noise assessments were not identified. The campaign did not respond to questions.

name: Gary Cordery
summary: No clear public position on data centers was identified in the material reviewed. The campaign did not respond to email requests for comment.

name: Josh Green
summary: No clear public position on data center development was identified in the material reviewed. The campaign did not respond to repeated requests for comment.

name: Brad Little
summary: The incumbent supports data center development but says facilities should bear their increased energy costs. He signed a sales tax exemption for data centers in 2020 and a 2026 law limiting their water use. The law does not require public disclosure of the amount used. Little has not explicitly stated his position  on a moratorium.

name: Terri Pickens
summary: In a direct response to the Project's questions, the lawyer said she supports public reporting of data center water use, separate utility rates and use requirements and noise assessments. She said she not support tax breaks for data center projects. In a Sept. 1 post to Facebook, Pickens said data centers should only receive special tax treatment "when there is a clear, measurable benefit to Idaho." She does not support a moratorium on data centers.

name: Darren Bailey
summary: The former state legislator says data centers are necessary but opposes tax incentives for them. Public positions on mandatory water-use reporting and noise assessments were not identified in the material reviewed.

name: JB Pritzker
summary: The incumbent has paused tax incentives for data centers and called for stronger rules. Proposed legislation would require facilities to pay their energy and water costs, report water use, meet air-quality standards and support renewable energy. It would also prioritize residential and other business customers during periods of high demand. The proposal failed to advance before the Legislature adjourned. A position on noise assessments is unclear.

name: Zach Lahn
summary: The farmer and businessman supports a statewide moratorium, water-use reporting and eliminating tax breaks. He wants data center companies to pay for their electricity and address environmental concerns. He has not said whether he supports noise assessment requirements for data centers.

name: Rob Sand
summary: The state auditor supports water-use reporting, eliminating tax incentives and requiring data centers to cover utility cost increases. He also favors consumer protections, public hearings and setback requirements to address noise before projects are built, though has not stated whether he supports noise assessment requirements for projects. His position on a data center moratorium remains unclear.

name: Ty Masterson
summary: The state Senate leader opposes a statewide moratorium and favors local decision-making. He has supported data center tax incentives and has not clearly stated a position on public water-use reporting or noise assessments.

name: Cindy Holscher
summary: The state legislator supports a statewide moratorium, public water-use reporting and separate utility rates. Although she previously voted for data center tax incentives, she says she has changed her position after hearing from constituents. A position on noise assessments is unclear.

name: Bobby Charles
summary: The former assistant secretary of state supports a statewide moratorium, citing resident costs and environmental effects, particularly on rivers. He says data centers must produce their own electricity. Positions on public water-use reporting, tax incentives and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Hannah Pingree
summary: The former state policy official supports a statewide moratorium, citing environmental concerns and the need to reduce electricity costs. Pingree supports requirements that data centers produce their own clean energy and seeks to protect local ratepayers. She has criticized the governor’s veto of a proposed moratorium.

name: Dan Cox
summary: The former state delegate supports an immediate statewide ban on data center construction, citing energy demand and risks to farms, water and communities. He opposes tax breaks and says residents should not pay for power infrastructure. Specific positions on water reporting and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Wes Moore
summary: The incumbent opposes a statewide moratorium and favors leaving siting decisions to counties. His executive order calls for public tracking of power and water use, noise and community-impact reviews, and requiring facilities to pay for grid upgrades. He also wants to end sales tax breaks for data centers.

name: Michael Minogue
summary: The former military officer and businessman supports requiring data centers to pay their own electricity costs and supports a temporary moratorium on new development. He opposes tax incentives. A position on local zoning and water-use reporting needs confirmation from the underlying sources.

name: Maura Healey
summary: The incumbent supports local approval before data centers can be built and opposes projects that lack it. The spreadsheet’s answer fields also indicate support for zoning/local approval and opposition to tax incentives. Water reporting, utility requirements and a moratorium need further verification against the linked executive announcement.

name: John James
summary: The U.S. representative favors local control over data center siting and opposes a statewide ban in general. He says development should protect natural resources and prevent pollution, but specific requirements remain unclear.

name: Jocelyn Benson
summary: The secretary of state supports a moratorium until safeguards are established, opposes data center tax breaks and wants facilities to pay for their power. She also supports public hearings, union agreements for well-paying jobs and proof that projects will protect natural resources. Zoning details need confirmation.

name: Lisa Demuth
summary: The state House speaker supports tax incentives and opposes separate utility rates for data centers, while saying facilities should pay their own costs and follow the same rules as local businesses. The material reviewed does not establish a clear position on water-use reporting.

name: Amy Klobuchar
summary: The U.S. senator has supported federal legislation addressing data center water use, opposes tax breaks and favors local decision-making. She voted against separating utility rates for data centers. Her position on zoning requirements was not established.

name: Jim Pillen
summary: The incumbent’s campaign emphasizes tax relief, agriculture and business growth. The material provided does not establish specific positions on data center water reporting, utility requirements, a moratorium, tax incentives or noise assessments.

name: Lynne Walz
summary: The former state legislator’s campaign emphasizes transparency, affordability and livable communities. The material provided does not establish specific positions on data center water reporting, utility requirements, a moratorium, tax incentives or noise assessments.

name: Joe Lombardo
summary: The incumbent supports continued data center development with additional conditions for facilities receiving tax abatements. His executive order addresses water, electricity, grid reliability, school funding, transparency and community impacts. He opposes a statewide moratorium and supports keeping incentives available under stricter requirements. A specific statewide noise-assessment mandate is not established.

name: Aaron Ford
summary: The incumbent attorney general supports public reporting of water use and requiring data centers to pay for their energy and grid infrastructure. He has proposed pausing new tax breaks while the state audits existing facilities, but has not endorsed a statewide moratorium. Other positions should be checked against the campaign’s full policy materials.

name: Kelly Ayotte
summary: The incumbent has shifted from supporting data center development to saying projects do not currently make sense because of energy, environmental and siting concerns. She has publicly discussed a statewide moratorium. She previously signed a law allowing off-grid energy providers.

name: Cinde Warmington
summary: The former state executive supports a statewide moratorium, citing the lack of rules on energy, water, noise and local control. Her campaign says safeguards are needed to protect communities and keep energy affordable. Her platform requires data centers to cover the cost of their expenses and ensure the grid can cover the load of data center projects.

name: Gregg Hull
summary: The former mayor of Rio Rancho opposes a statewide moratorium and supports tax incentives for data centers. He favors separate utility rates and says communities should be able to reject projects that do not fit local needs. Public positions on water-use reporting and noise assessments were not identified.

name: Deb Haaland
summary: The former U.S. interior secretary supports annual water-use reporting for high-demand industries, requiring data centers to build renewable energy infrastructure and cover their costs. Her plan calls for a moratorium on new large-scale projects until safeguards are established.

name: Bruce Blakeman
summary: The Nassau County executive has criticized the statewide moratorium, calling it unreasonable, and says data centers are important to New York’s competitiveness. The campaign did not respond to questions about his specific policy positions.

name: Kathy Hochul
summary: The incumbent signed a 2026 executive order establishing a one-year pause on state-level data center permitting. It calls for separate utility rates and use requirements, noise assessments and an end to tax incentives. A position on public water-use reporting remains unclear.

name: Vivek Ramaswamy
summary: The businessman supports a temporary halt to new approvals until requirements are in place. He wants data centers to pay full property taxes and nearby residents’ electricity costs, recycle and minimize water use, and meet environmental standards.

name: Amy Acton
summary: The former state health director supports a conditional pause on data center approvals and requiring facilities to cover all their utility costs. She also favors stronger environmental, labor and community protections for data center development.  She says she wants to "rein in" incentives for data centers and add clawback provisions, but it is unclear whether she is still supportive of the measures.

name: Mike Mazzei
summary: The financial-services executive supports separate utility rates and requirements, requiring data centers to provide their own electricity and cooling systems, and local approval of industrial sites. He opposes special property tax breaks and a statewide moratorium. Positions on water-use reporting and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Cyndi Munson
summary: The state House minority leader supports a moratorium on new projects until statewide standards are set. She favors water protections and separate utility treatment for large data centers, opposes tax incentives and helped advance legislation requiring separate rates for large energy users. A position on noise assessments is unclear.

name: Christine Drazan
summary: The state senator supports a statewide moratorium and says she would protect communities from unwanted data center development. She has also emphasized the need for local protections. Drazan voted against the POWER Act, which placed special rates on data centers and large-load facilities, indicating her non-support of regulatory measures. She has criticized existing tax breaks, but said she would not axe incentives for data centers, according to reporting by Oregon Public Broadcasting. Her data center platform says centers have received "special tax treatment" though she voted against a proposal to roll back a tax incentive benefitting data centers and other businesses.

name: Tina Kotek
summary: The incumbent supports prohibiting new data center development until statewide standards are in place. She has also supported legislation intended to ensure large energy users bear their own costs rather than shifting them to households and other businesses.

name: Stacy Garrity
summary: The state treasurer supports water-use reporting, separate utility rates and requirements, and ending tax incentives for data centers. She has called for facilities to provide their own energy and use a separate water supply, and supports a temporary moratorium while officials develop a path forward.

name: Josh Shapiro
summary: The incumbent opposes a moratorium and supports public water-use reporting, noise assessments and requiring data centers to provide and pay for their utility use. An executive order makes existing tax incentives conditional on local support and environmental safeguards.

name: Aaron Guckian
summary: One of three who responded to this survey, the candidate said in an email response that he supported public water-use reporting, separate utility rates and requirements, and noise assessments, but opposed a statewide moratorium. He favors local siting decisions and opposes tax incentives unless they deliver measurable benefits, including permanent jobs and a positive return on public investment.

name: Helena Buonanno Foulkes
summary: The former retail and pharmacy executive favors regulating data centers rather than imposing an outright moratorium. Foulkes said she would not sign a sales tax exemption for data center equipment, which was part of a proposal in the General Assembly that sought to bring data centers to the state. She supports measures that require large-load users to "pay their own way" for energy costs. She says the state should explore ways to keep costs low for ratepayers, including specific electricty rates for data centers, as linked in her No False Choices plan.

name: Ken Block
summary: The independent candidate’s platform has focused on preventing tax increases and wasteful government spending. His platform has not established specific positions on data center development or related safeguards.

name: Alan Wilson
summary: The state attorney general favors leaving data center decisions to local communities rather than imposing broad statewide rules. Like is opponent, Wilson supports a "bring your own energy" approach. His position on water reporting, tax incentives and noise assessments remains unclear. In a gubernatorial debate on Oct. 6, the candidate said he would require data centers to implement noise mitigations.

name: Jermaine Johnson
summary: The state representative supports a moratorium on data center construction until a transparent plan protects communities, infrastructure and energy resources. He has promoted a “bring your own energy” approach for data center companies.

name: Larry Rhoden
summary: The incumbent, a former rancher and welder, has emphasized low taxes, signed legislation requiring covered data centers to pay their power-related costs, notify local water providers of their needs, and respect local authority to regulate or ban projects.

name: Dan Ahlers
summary: The state legislator has focused on rural communities, education, affordable housing, rural health care and wages. The material provided does not establish specific positions on data center development or related safeguards.

name: Marsha Blackburn
summary: The U.S. senator supports data center development as an economic driver but favors careful siting and protections against shifting energy and infrastructure costs to other customers. She has supported disclosure of expected water use and community impacts and opposes a statewide moratorium. Positions on tax incentives and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Jerri Green
summary: The Memphis City Council member supports a statewide moratorium on new data centers and ending state incentives. She favors stronger standards for water, energy, environmental impacts, infrastructure costs, zoning and community input, and says companies should cover their costs. Her published positions do not specify support for water-use reporting, separate utility rates or noise assessments.

name: Greg Abbott
summary: The incumbent supports requiring data centers to pay for their electricity infrastructure and reducing tax breaks. He has backed temporary pauses on some approvals while impacts are reviewed, but not a permanent statewide ban. He wants state officials to assess effects on water, electricity, traffic and communities.

name: Gina Hinojosa
summary: The state representative supports a temporary halt on new data centers until stronger safeguards are established. She wants companies to disclose water and electricity use, cover their costs, end tax breaks and give communities more say over siting.

name: Phil Scott
summary: The incumbent would support a moratorium on data centers while the state evaluates steps taken by the federal government, according to reporting by the Vermont Digger. In May, Scott vetoed a bill aimed at regulating data center development, which included power regulations. He said the bill could be too broadly applied, but would support a version of the bill that could not be as broadly imp

name: Amanda Janoo
summary: The candidate supports a moratorium on AI data centers, according to a cited Sierra Club post. The current summary does not establish her other policy positions; verify the cited post and any additional campaign statements before publication.

name: Tom Tiffany
summary: The incumbent opposes a statewide moratorium and favors tighter rules for development, but does not support separate utility rates and requirements. Positions on water-use reporting and noise assessments are unclear.

name: David Crowley
summary: The incumbent opposes a statewide moratorium but supports stronger regulations, public water-use reporting and separate utility rates and requirements. A position on noise assessments is unclear.

name: Eric Barlow
summary: The former state legislator opposes a statewide moratorium and says data centers could benefit the state if they use local energy and little or no local water. Positions on tax incentives and noise assessments are unclear.

name: Ken Casner
summary: In direct responses to the project’s questions, the candidate supported public water-use reporting, separate utility rates and requirements, a statewide moratorium, tax incentives and noise assessments.
